claims.sourceSpan: SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026''.

claims.claim: Division H section 102 provides that the time covered by the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 is considered to include the period beginning on or about January 31, 2026, during which there occurred a lapse in appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: For the purposes of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 (division A of Public Law 119-37), the time covered by such division shall be considered to include the period which began on or about January 31, 2026, during which there occurred a lapse in appropriations.

claims.claim: The stop-gap in force was division A of Public Law 119-37, the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026
claims.sourceSpan: DIVISION A--CONTINUING APPROPRIATONS ACT, 2026

claims.claim: Section 106(3) of that CR set its expiration at January 30, 2026 — the day before the lapse began
claims.sourceSpan: (3) <<NOTE: Expiration date.>> January 30, 2026.

claims.claim: Section 106 of that CR runs its funding until whichever of three listed events first occurs
claims.sourceSpan: appropriations and funds made available and authority granted pursuant to this Act shall be available until whichever of the following first occurs:

claims.claim: CRS: agencies lacking funding after the expiration of regular appropriations or a CR experience a "funding gap"
claims.sourceSpan: When federal agencies and programs lack funding after the expiration of regular appropriations or a CR, the agencies and programs experience a “funding gap.”

claims.claim: CRS: if no new appropriations are enacted in time, agencies are legally required to cease operations, known as a government shutdown, except where the law authorizes continued activities
claims.sourceSpan: If no new appropriations are enacted in time to continue operations for such agencies or programs, then the agencies are legally required to cease operations (known as a “government shutdown”), except in certain situations when the law authorizes continued activities.

claims.claim: A federal fiscal year begins October 1 and ends September 30 of the following year, and is designated by the calendar year in which it ends — so FY2026 ran October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026
claims.sourceSpan: The fiscal year for the federal government begins on October 1 of each year and ends on September 30 of the following year; it is designated by the calendar year in which it ends.

claims.claim: REMOVED: "avoiding a government shutdown that had been threatened as Congress struggled to pass individual appropriations bills through the fall." Contradicted by the law's own Division H section 102, which records a lapse in appropriations beginning on or about January 31, 2026 — three days before the bill was signed.

REMOVED: "The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 organized funding into the standard twelve appropriations subcommittees" followed by all twelve names. The enrolled text has nine divisions of which five are annual appropriations acts; seven of the twelve subcommittees appear nowhere in this law.

REMOVED: "Each division covers one subcommittee's jurisdiction. The bill also includes a General Provisions division that applies government-wide." There is no government-wide General Provisions division; Division E title VII is titled General Provisions--Government-wide and sits inside one division.

REMOVED: "Overall discretionary spending in H.R. 7148 was set at levels consistent with the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (Pub. L. 118-5) caps — the deal reached in June 2023 to raise the debt ceiling in exchange for statutory spending limits." The phrase "Fiscal Responsibility Act" appears nowhere in the enrolled text; the 16 references to Public Law 118-5 are all bare cross-references to "section 103(b) of division A" used as a scorekeeping treatment for certain infrastructure balances. No stored source names, dates or characterises the Act, and none states this law's levels were consistent with any caps.

REMOVED: "Defense discretionary spending received an increase relative to FY2025 levels, consistent with the pattern of bipartisan agreement on defense spending." No FY2025 defense baseline is stored and none was fetchable; the characterisation of bipartisan agreement rests on nothing.

REMOVED: "with some accounts — particularly at the IRS and EPA — subject to the reduction riders that have characterized appropriations debates in recent years." The Environmental Protection Agency is named once in 34,575 lines of the enrolled text, in an unrelated coordination clause; Interior-Environment is one of the seven subcommittees this law does not carry. No rider or FY2025 comparison for the IRS exists in the text or in any stored source.
REMOVED: "H.R. 7148 contained a large number of general provisions across its twelve divisions." It has nine.

REMOVED: "A rider rides on the vote for the whole package; it is not voted on separately." Contradicted by the site's own sourced omnibus-vs-minibus explainer and by the H.R. 6938 action record, where the House voted separately on retaining each division. Replaced with what H.R. 7148's own record shows.

REMOVED: the whole "What It Doesn't Include" section — "Provisions related to specific authorizations, supplemental funding packages for ongoing international situations, and certain domestic policy changes that couldn't achieve bipartisan support were left for separate legislation or deferred to FY2027 negotiations" and "The absence of something from an omnibus is often as significant as what's in it… has been effectively repealed for the current fiscal year." No source names any omitted provision, and no stored authority supports the repeal characterisation.

REMOVED: "Given recent history, the probability of individual bills passing on time is low; another continuing resolution or consolidated bill is the more likely outcome." A prediction with no source. Replaced with the recorded state of the two FY2027 measures and the public-law list.

REMOVED from the Primary Sources box and the JSON-LD citation list: the bare https://www.cbo.gov homepage and the https://www.govinfo.gov/app/collection/PLAW collection index. Neither sources any statement in the article. Replaced with CRS R47106, CRS R48731 and the GAO glossary, which do.

REMOVED (round 1, introduced by this audit and caught by a hostile Sonnet pass): "Divisions I and J are extenders — provisions that move an expiration date rather than appropriate money." The gloss is the audit's own invention and the text contradicts it: Division I section 5016 grants authority to raise the H-2B cap, 5011 pushes the Parole Commission to 2031, and Division J creates an Abraham Accords Office in the FDA (6611), mandates a Medicaid/CHIP enrollment process (6101) and imposes PBM oversight and rebate pass-through (title VII). Replaced with the law's own division titles, real examples of both kinds, and CRS IN12324, which says these divisions carry extensions "as well as legislation establishing new programs, projects, or activities."

REMOVED (round 1): "That division-per-bill structure is how any package is assembled." Overstated — the audited omnibus-vs-minibus explainer, sourced to CRS IN12324, says each included bill is USUALLY its own division. Reworded to "usually".

REMOVED (round 1, my own fresh read): "seven named State Department headings" in Division F section 7072. Subsection (d) is a USAID bureau heading (Bureau for Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance) and (e) is the Millennium Challenge Corporation, an independent agency. Reworded to headings from prior Acts making appropriations for the Department of State, foreign operations and related programs, which is what the text says.

REMOVED (round 1): "the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2027" as H.R. 8646's name. Congress.gov's assigned short title uses the singular "Agency"; the bill's own engrossed text has no short-title section at all and its long title uses the plural "Agencies". Replaced with the bill's own long title so the article does not adjudicate between them.

FLAG, not acted on (bill lane, not this batch): data/cache.json's Division G summary for 119-HR-7148 describes the UNRWA bar as reaching "all U.S. funds — from this Act and from prior fiscal years". The provision reaches funds appropriated or otherwise made available by division F or by other Acts making appropriations for the Department of State, foreign operations and related programs — not divisions A, B, D or E. The article follows the statute, not the cache entry.

ADJUDICATED, no change: a hostile pass read data/cache.json's "National Flood Insurance Program (retroactively to January 30, 2026)" as contradicting the article's "from September 30, 2023 to September 30, 2026". Both are right and they describe different things — section 5004(a) and (b) strike the 2023 date and insert 2026; section 5004(c)(2) is a separate effective-date rule making the section take effect as if enacted on January 30, 2026. The article now states both.

REMOVED: "Consolidated appropriations bills are also the preferred vehicle for policy riders — statutory changes that couldn't pass as standalone legislation — attached to a bill that has to pass, because there is no clean way to strip them from it." Unsourced characterisation. Replaced with CRS R47106 on general provisions and House Rule XXI / Senate Rule XVI, plus the law's own examples.

claims.claim: REMOVED (round 2, my own fresh read of the corrected draft): five characterisations the sources do not make — "keeps all of it off the books" (PAYGO scorekeeping is a budget-enforcement mechanism, not "the books"); "closing the gap the lapse had opened" (the statute gives no reason for the retroactive effective date); "the labels understate them, and CRS says that is the pattern" (CRS describes what omnibus divisions carry, not what this law's labels do); "and stopped there" (replaced with the recorded absence of Senate action); and "appropriating for" where the statute says "making appropriations for".

notes: First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, run as Phase B session 5 of the article audit sweep. Rebuilt against the enrolled text of P.L. 119-75 and the stored CRS/GAO sources the omnibus-vs-minibus explainer already uses, so the two pages now agree. Twelve claim families were REMOVED rather than softened (see the removed.* rows): the article had described a nine-division, five-bill package as a twelve-subcommittee omnibus that averted a shutdown, when the law's own Division H records a lapse in appropriations three days before signing. ROUND 1: three hostile Sonnet passes (source-only; cross-page/editorial/structural; omission/overclaim). Two REFUSALS produced real blocking findings, one of them a defect this audit itself introduced — a Divisions I and J gloss ("provisions that move an expiration date") the text contradicts. Sec. 5021 PAYGO exemption added. My own fresh read then found what none of the three did: Public Law 119-86 Division B section 102 records a SECOND lapse in appropriations beginning on or about 2026-02-14, the day after the date this law inserted. ROUND 2 (full re-verification of the corrected draft, hostile Sonnet, source-only): ZERO factual discrepancies across the whole article — every quotation, dollar figure, vote tally, division/section cite, the two-lapse spine and the eleven-of-twelve arithmetic confirmed exact against stored text. Its one REFUSE was on datePublished/dateModified, which publish-article --refresh stamps after the check; disposed of as out of scope, and confirmed correct after publishing. ROUND 3 (targeted, on a frozen file, the six sentences round 2 never saw): SIGN OFF, 7 of 7 PASS with line-cited source, including a programmatic absence scan of all 288,039 characters of Division J.
